To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the utilization of reward systems varies between countries; (2) there is evidence of a ‘Japanese model’ in terms of the utilization of financial incentives; (3) there is a clear difference between multinational enterprises and domestic firms, with MNEs being more likely to utilize financial incentives.

the use of share schemes and performance-related pay varies significantly between countries, with Japan being a clear exception to the general pattern of the use of share ownership and performance-related pay being more prevalent in liberal market economies than in coordinated market economies.
there are significant differences in reward systems between countries, but also within countries.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the extent to which reward system practices vary according to the institutional context in which they are embedded, and the extent to which multinational enterprises are able to adopt practices which differ from the local norm.

the extent to which reward practices vary according to the institutional context in which firms are located, the extent to which multinational enterprises are different from domestic firms, and the extent to which the institutional context of the parent firm is a more important determinant of reward practices than the institutional context of a subsidiary.
the extent to which the institutional and national context continues to influence reward practices within multinational enterprises.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence suggests the presence of both convergence and diversity in reward practices across the world.

there is a clear and significant difference in the use of share schemes and performance-related pay between the two varieties of capitalism and, furthermore, that this difference is more marked in the case of multinational enterprises.

there is a clear relationship between the type of reward system and the variety of capitalism in which the firm operates, and that multinational enterprises are more likely to adopt a performance related pay system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of reward practices in MNEs is influenced by the national institutional environment, and that MNEs are more likely to use reward systems that are similar to those in their home country.
, while the use of financial incentive schemes is widespread across the world, there are clear differences in the way they are utilized.
there is a clear relationship between the institutional context and reward practices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the institutional context continues to be an important driver of reward system design and implementation.
the institutional context of reward systems continues to matter, and that the institutional context is not the same for MNEs as it is for their domestic peers.

, despite the increasing globalization of markets, and the increasing presence of multinational enterprises in many countries, there are significant differences in the use of reward systems between countries, and between multinationals and local enterprises.
